title: The Phasor Bench
summary: Convert rms and peak values, find bulb resistance and AC power in a resistor, and read a phasor.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 7.2, AC voltage applied to a resistor
learningOutcome: The student can convert between rms and peak values, find the resistance and currents of a rated bulb, find the average and peak power in a resistor, and read an instantaneous value from a phasor.

levels.title: A rated bulb
levels.adds: Baseline: ratings are rms values, P = V²/R, and the peak is √2 times the rms (Example 7.1).
hints: The stated voltage is the rms value.
The peak voltage is √2 times the rms voltage.

levels.title: rms and peak
levels.adds: New idea: V_rms = v_m/√2 and i_m = √2 I_rms (Ex 7.2).
hints: The rms value is the peak divided by √2.
The peak is the rms value times √2.
Check which one of the two you are given.

levels.title: Power over a cycle
levels.adds: New idea: power in a resistor never goes negative; the average is half the peak (Ex 7.1).
hints: The average power is V_rms I_rms.
The largest power at any instant is twice the average.

levels.title: Read the phasor
levels.adds: Apply it: v = v_m sin ωt, and a resistor’s current is in phase with the voltage (Section 7.3).
hints: v_m is √2 times the rms voltage.
v = v_m sin ωt at the given angle.
In a resistor, v and i rise and fall together.

misconceptions: The stated 220 V of the mains is the peak voltage
The average power in a resistor is zero over a cycle
The current in a resistor lags the voltage
